title: Implement a queue using an array — enqueue (add at back), dequeue (remove from front).
shortTitle: Implement a Queue using an Array

s1_definition.profdef: An array-backed queue stores elements in a fixed-size array and uses two index pointers, front and rear, to track the head and tail of the line. Enqueue places an element at the rear position and advances the rear pointer; dequeue reads the element at the front position and advances the front pointer. A circular (ring buffer) design wraps the pointers around using the modulo operator so the array space is reused and no shifting is needed.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of a row of numbered pigeon-holes on the wall at the National Bank of India. Rajesh's request goes into hole 0, Priya's into hole 1, the next into hole 2. A "front" sticky note points to the oldest unprocessed hole and a "rear" sticky note points to the next empty hole. When a teller processes the oldest request, the front note moves forward. When the rear reaches the end of the wall, it wraps back to the start if earlier holes are free. Nobody physically moves the papers — only the sticky notes move.
s1_definition.oneliner: An array queue is a ring of slots where a front pointer and a rear pointer chase each other around using modulo.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** An array-backed queue stores elements in a fixed-size array and uses two index pointers, front and rear, to track the head and tail of the line. Enqueue places an element at the rear position and advances the rear pointer; dequeue reads the element at the front position and advances the front pointer. A circular (ring buffer) design wraps the pointers around using the modulo operator so the array space is reused and no shifting is needed.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of a row of numbered pigeon-holes on the wall at the National Bank of India. Rajesh's request goes into hole 0, Priya's into hole 1, the next into hole 2. A "front" sticky note points to the oldest unprocessed hole and a "rear" sticky note points to the next empty hole. When a teller processes the oldest request, the front note moves forward. When the rear reaches the end of the wall, it wraps back to the start if earlier holes are free. Nobody physically moves the papers — only the sticky notes move.

**One line to remember:** An array queue is a ring of slots where a front pointer and a rear pointer chase each other around using modulo.

sections.s2_technical:
A naive array queue removes from the front by shifting every remaining element one step left, which costs O(n) per dequeue. The professional solution is a circular queue. Instead of shifting, we keep a `front` index and a `rear` index and move them forward, wrapping around with the modulo operator.

The `enqueue` operation first checks if the queue is full. For example, `if (count == capacity) throw new IllegalStateException("Queue full")` protects us from overflow. Then it writes the value at the rear slot with `items[rear] = value` and advances the pointer with `rear = (rear + 1) % capacity`, and finally `count++`. The modulo is what makes the pointer wrap back to index 0 after it reaches the end.

The `dequeue` operation checks if the queue is empty with `if (count == 0) throw new NoSuchElementException()`, then reads the front slot using `BigDecimal value = items[front]`, advances with `front = (front + 1) % capacity`, decrements `count--`, and returns the value. Reading and advancing is O(1), which is the big win over shifting.

A senior-level nuance is tracking size with a separate `count` variable rather than trying to compute size from `front` and `rear` alone. When front equals rear, you cannot tell if the queue is empty or completely full without the count, so the explicit counter removes that ambiguity. In high-performance systems, this exact ring buffer design is used in logging frameworks and network buffers because it never allocates after construction.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India has a cheque-clearing station that can hold only a fixed number of cheques in its physical tray at once, say five. Cheques arrive at the back of the tray and the clerk picks from the front. If the tray is full, new cheques must wait outside. We need a fixed-capacity, first-in-first-out holder. This is exactly a bounded array-backed queue — fixed capacity, add at rear, remove from front.

Problem 2 — The clerk processes cheques and frees slots, and new cheques keep arriving. We do not want to keep shifting all cheques forward every time one is removed because that wastes effort. This is why we use a circular queue, where the free slots at the front get reused by wrapping the rear pointer around.

In our mini-project we build an `ArrayQueue` of `String` cheque numbers with a fixed capacity. We enqueue several cheques, dequeue a couple, then enqueue more to prove the pointers wrap around correctly. The code has an `ArrayQueue` class with enqueue, dequeue, peek, isEmpty, and isFull, and a main demo that exercises the wrap-around behaviour and logs it.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: a tray of capacity 3. We enqueue CHQ-1001, CHQ-1002, CHQ-1003, then dequeue twice, then enqueue CHQ-1004 and CHQ-1005.

Step 1: Enqueue CHQ-1001. It goes to index 0. Rear advances to 1. Count is 1.

Step 2: Enqueue CHQ-1002 at index 1, rear moves to 2, count 2. Enqueue CHQ-1003 at index 2, rear wraps to 0 using modulo, count 3. The tray is now full.

Step 3: Dequeue. We read index 0 which is CHQ-1001, front advances to 1, count drops to 2. Index 0 is now free.

Step 4: Dequeue again. We read index 1 which is CHQ-1002, front moves to 2, count 1. Index 1 is now free.

Step 5: Enqueue CHQ-1004. Rear is at 0 (it wrapped earlier), so CHQ-1004 lands in the freed index 0. Rear advances to 1, count 2.

Step 6: Enqueue CHQ-1005 into freed index 1, rear advances to 2, count 3. The pointers successfully wrapped and reused space without any shifting.

Step 7: We drain the remaining cheques from the front in order: CHQ-1003, CHQ-1004, CHQ-1005.

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Array-Backed Circular Queue ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Ring Buffer: modulo-wrapped front/rear pointers reuse slots  │
  │  Bounded Buffer: fixed capacity provides natural back-pressure│
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ───────────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: ArrayQueue only stores and orders cheques                │
  │  O: capacity is a constructor parameter, no code change to    │
  │     resize behaviour                                          │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ────────────────────────────────────────

  ┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
  │           ArrayQueue                │
  │  ────────────────────────────────── │
  │  - items: String[]                  │  fixed backing array
  │  - capacity: int                    │
  │  - front: int                       │  oldest element index
  │  - rear: int                        │  next free index
  │  - count: int                       │  disambiguates empty/full
  │  ────────────────────────────────── │
  │  + enqueue(s): void                 │  O(1), throws if full
  │  + dequeue(): String                │  O(1), throws if empty
  │  + peek(): String                   │
  │  + isEmpty(): boolean               │
  │  + isFull(): boolean                │
  └─────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── State Diagram: Slot Lifecycle ─────────────────────────

  [EMPTY slot] ──enqueue──→ [OCCUPIED] ──dequeue──→ [EMPTY, reusable]

  ── Call Chain ────────────────────────────────────────────

  1. enqueue("CHQ-1001") → items[rear]=value; rear=(rear+1)%cap; count++
  2. dequeue()           → read items[front]; front=(front+1)%cap; count--
  3. isFull()            → count == capacity
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
To implement a queue using an array, I use a fixed-size array together with two index pointers, one called front pointing to the oldest element and one called rear pointing to the next free slot, plus a count of how many elements are currently stored. Enqueue writes the new element at the rear slot and advances the rear pointer, while dequeue reads the element at the front slot and advances the front pointer.

The key trick I always highlight is making the queue circular. A naive array queue removes from the front by shifting every remaining element one position left, which costs linear time on every dequeue. Instead, I advance the pointers and wrap them around using the modulo operator, so freed slots at the front get reused by the rear. This makes both enqueue and dequeue constant time operations.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India, I used this bounded circular queue for a cheque-clearing station that can physically hold only a fixed number of cheques at once. Cheques enter at the rear and the clerk processes them from the front, and when the tray is full the system naturally applies back-pressure and makes new cheques wait. Because the ring buffer reuses freed slots, the clerk can keep working steadily without the system ever having to shuffle cheques around.

One subtle point I make sure to mention is why I keep a separate count variable. When the front index equals the rear index, you cannot tell whether the queue is completely empty or completely full just from the pointers, because both situations look identical. The explicit count removes that ambiguity cleanly. This same ring buffer design shows up in real production systems like logging frameworks and network buffers, precisely because it is fast and never needs to allocate memory after it is created.
